newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmiri town flocks to first polls in nine years.
newsitem.headline: Kashmiri town flocks to first polls in nine years.

text.p: The only violence in this Kashmiri town on Saturday occurred when supporters of rival politicians traded blows inside a polling station.
The threat of danger hung over much of Jammu and Kashmir state, where 200,000 security officers were deployed to protect voters in the first state assembly elections in nine years.
Authorities said at least four people died in scattered violence and cross-border firing in the Himalayan region.
In contrast with Pattan, some voting booths in the scenic Kashmir Valley, focus of a six-year-old rebellion, were empty.
But in Pattan, 25 km (15 miles) northwest of the state's summer capital, Srinagar, hundreds of men and women crowded freely around polling booths, eager to cast votes.
"We want peace. That's why we voted," Tariq Zargar, a 22-year-old worker at an ice cream factory, told Reuters.
A.K. Lahiri, a polling official who travelled from India's capital, New Delhi, to help supervise the voting, said only one incident marred the almost carnival atmosphere.
"When the Congress party candidate came to vote, activists backing his rival shouted abusive language and supporters of both candidates exchanged blows," Lahiri said.
"Nothing wrong with that," he added.
Lahiri said 150 people were lined up before the polls opened at 7.00 a.m. (0130 GMT).
"I have never seen this before. People are so enthusiastic to have a chance to vote after a lapse of so many years."
Lahiri said 582 of 771 voters on his roll had cast ballots when only two hours of polling remained.
The enthusiasm was explained partly by the apparent popularity of Abdul Rashid Shaheen, a former state minister and Janata Dal national Indian party candidate.
"He has helped us a lot and stayed here during the six years of militancy," said local resident Shoket Butt. "He would visit families' homes whenever their loved ones were killed."
Several voters said they were choosing a middle path between separatist militants and a security crackdown.
"We wanted freedom when militancy first started," said Afrooza Sofi, a 21-year-old student wearing a traditional black Moslem veil, or burqua.
"Then militancy turned to terrorism. We suffered so much that whatever the next government brings us will be better than what we have gone through," she added.
More than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since the revolt erupted in 1990.
Mohammad Aslam, a 32-year-old biology lecturer at the town's college, said his uncle was among the 100 or so citizens of Pattan, with a population of 8,000, who had died.
"We are fed up with the gun culture here," Aslam said.
"We can get freedom through the government. We can raise our voices to any corner of the world. But we must have a channel. The government is the channel," he said.
Mohammad Ashrif, a 32-year-old student, said he expected the new state government, which will take office when the four-phase election ends later this month, to spur economic development.
"Let the militants go to Pakistan and see," he said.
"We are fed up with guns, whether they are the army's or the militants'. They have been misused."
